#9907. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

Extract text and tables from document images

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#9905. Making Games in Go: Entity Component System (ECS)

Twice a year, we run an online hands-on training on Event-Driven patterns in Go. The time has come! Learn more.

MiÅosz SmÃ³ÅkaCo-founder of Three Dots Labs. Creator of Watermill. Author of Go With The Domain.

I started my last post on making games by saying gamedev is a great hobby for when you don’t do as much coding day-to-day. A few years later, many of us see even less code, so it feels like a good time to give it another shot. This time I talk about ECS, a data-oriented way to structure games. I show it on a small game you can play right in this post.

But first, the elephant in the room: Don’t AI agents one-shot full games now?

Sure. Why would that stop you from learning something new?

Just for fun, focus on the process instead of the outcome. Make a game your way. It’ll make you want to scream “LOOK WHAT I HAVE CREATED!” like Tom Hanks in Cast Away. (Note: there’s no audience in that scene, which is very accurate.)

I find making games fun for at least two reasons:

Using AI takes the fun out of tinkering with the code (reason #1). But it lets you see the results quicker and try bigger projects (reason #2). There’s no wrong way to have fun, so pick whatever fits your mood.

Even if you use AI, it’s still worth learning the foundations. I found it easier to steer agents when they work on a project where I had already put the scaffolding in place. They’re much better at imitation than coming up with something new. (I share the patterns I give agents at the end.)

Learning software concepts isn’t only about the code. It also changes how you think about projects. You know what systems are in place, how the elements interact, and what a good solution would be. I care more than ever about keeping my mental models sharp now that AI can produce infinite output that’s worthless unless someone decides otherwise.

The usual disclaimer: I’m a hobbyist making tiny 2D games. I do it for fun, and have never shipped a professional game. I write about what has worked for me, and it could be something dumb. (If that’s the case, let me know in the comments!)

Previously, I described a simple approach to working with game objects. Each object is a struct and has its own Update() and Draw() methods. In the game loop, we iterate over all the objects and call their methods.

This is a good start. It’s easy to follow how the game works and to add new objects. But as the game becomes more complex, it gets messy. The Update methods get long. You need to pass many references around, because objects don’t know about other objects. Some logic doesn’t clearly belong to any one object.

Another challenge in many games is that objects have similar traits, but aren’t quite the same thing. For example, a player character, an NPC, and an enemy are very similar objects, but also completely different gameplay-wise. They all have health points, move in the game world, collide with the terrain, and so on. But one is controlled by the player, one you can talk to to accept a quest, and one attacks you on sight.

One way to approach this is with some kind of inheritance (or embedding in Go). You create a basic Object with all common traits, then extend it with more specific entities.

But what if you want an NPC to turn hostile after an interaction? Or if you want the player to sometimes talk to the enemy? Or if you want to briefly take control over any of them? The inheritance model stops working, and you need workarounds that can get ugly.

I’ve been trying to figure this out, and I discovered the Entity Component System (ECS) architecture. It became my go-to approach for making games. I’m using the Donburi ECS library in Go together with the Ebitengine 2D game engine. Both are super fun to work with.

You may see ECS mentioned for performance reasons (storing components of one type together in memory makes iterating over them fast), but for me, the best part is the mental model shift. You split the game into small building blocks with clear responsibilities, so it’s easier to think about how it works. Keeping the data separate from the behavior is also an interesting idea that can help you approach other software projects.

If you want to follow along, I recommend reading the previous post first, where I explain the basics of Ebitengine.

In ECS, you split your game into three parts:

It’s like an extreme take on the Single Responsibility Principle. You clearly separate identity, data, and behavior in the code.

Let’s consider a trivial example to see how it works. We’ll display a grid of colorful tiles on the screen.

Each tile is an entity. An entity has no attributes by itself. Our game has 240 tiles. To give them meaning, we need to add components to them.

Let’s think of a minimal set of components the entity needs to appear as a tile on the screen.

Without a doubt, it needs a position in the game world, a pair of X and Y coordinates:

The other thing is the tile’s color. That’s a separate component:

Now, it would be natural to represent the tile like this:

But this isn’t what we want. As strange as it sounds, our game shouldn’t have a Tile struct. In ECS, there’s no place for a dedicated Tile type. Instead, we have generic entities made of components.

Let’s start working with Donburi primitives.

The structs we created above (PositionData and ColorData) hold the components’ data. We need to register component types as well. These are global variables:

To create an entity, we first have to create a world. It’s where Donburi tracks entities. Our game will have a single world with all entities living inside.

We create an entity for the tile with two components:

The entity lives inside the world from now on. We don’t need to keep track of it. Create returns an integer, because the entity is just an ID.

If we want to interact with the entity, we need to get its entry from the world:

The entry is a regular Go pointer, and it lets you do something useful with the entity, like reading or setting its component data.

At this point, the entity has two components attached: Position and Color (because we passed them to world.Create()). They hold zero values of their data structs.

We can read their data with the component’s Get method. This may be a bit unusual at first, since we call a method on the global component type, not directly on the entry.

To set a value, we can use SetValue like this:

Or by changing the struct in place, since Get returns a pointer:

We can also add or remove components and check if they exist:

The last part we need is systems. They are similar to regular Update functions.

As a reminder, here’s a minimal Ebitengine game (I’m skipping the Layout method, which isn’t relevant). Update is called every tick, usually 60 times per second, and Draw is called every frame.

In ECS, we move all the code from Update() and Draw() into systems. While Donburi has an experimental systems feature, I’ll stick to a manual but simpler approach here.

A system is an Update function that works within a given world.

We keep the world and a slice of systems in the Game struct. Then, we iterate over the systems in the Update method. Each tick, we update every system in the game.

We’ll also keep systems for drawing on the screen. I’ll call this kind of a system a Drawer, following the Go convention:

Note that a single system could expose both the Update and Draw methods.

What makes systems interesting is that each works on a subset of entities with specific components. A single system handles some particular logic relevant only to some entities.

For example, let’s say we want the color on our tiles to change continuously. So we add a system that iterates over all entities with the Color component and updates the Color value.

The key here is that, as far as the systems are aware, there’s no such thing as a tile. There are just entities with components on them. Often, systems are generic and work on a small number of components, without broader context of the entire game. This is unusual at first, but it gives you some interesting ways to design the game.

The first system we’ll add is the rendering system. It takes entities with Color and Position components and draws them on the screen. In this example, the tile size is constant, so that’s all the data we need from each entity.

To see where we’re heading, here’s the game with a debug inspector enabled. Hover over or tap a tile to see its data.

Let’s implement the rendering system. Systems fetch entities with Donburi queries. A query defines which components an entity must have and lets you iterate over the matches.

We create the query in the constructor and keep it as a field of the system struct, to avoid needless allocations every tick. The heavy lifting happens in Update or Draw.

Every frame, for each entity with a Position and a Color, the rendering system tints the white tile image with the entity’s color and draws it on the screen at the entity’s position.

Now we only need to create tiles with the correct positions and random colors while creating the world.

This example is trivial, of course. The rendering system is not that universal if all it can do is draw tiles. We’re moving to a more complex project soon, but first, let’s add two more systems to this example.

To make the tiles a bit less boring, let’s add a way to break them: when you click a tile, it should fall down the screen.

We’ll add a VelocitySystem, making the entities move. It’s a good example of a universal system in action. It updates the position and rotation of entities by the set values. We can forget it exists and set velocity on an entity we need to move.

Now, we need a system for detecting clicks on the tiles. First, let’s somehow mark the entities that can be clicked, so it’s more explicit. We’ll create a Clickable component.

This component has no data. We use it only to mark that the entity supports clicking on it. For components without data like this, we can use a shortcut from Donburi: a tag.

We need to include this tag along with the new components when creating an entity:

So once a mouse button is clicked (or the screen is tapped), we iterate over all clickable entities and check if they intersect with the pressed point. If so, we set a random velocity and rotation for the tile. That’s enough to get it moving, since the velocity system picks it up from there.

Finally, we remove the Clickable component, so that it’s not possible to click a falling tile again.

I also updated the rendering system to take rotation into account. You can see the full source on GitHub.

Hopefully you got a general idea of how Donburi works so far, but such a simple project doesn’t show the benefits of ECS well. Let’s look at another project.

We’ll simulate an aquarium, with the player controlling a friendly pufferfish. It grows by collecting bubbles and needs to avoid other fish around it. The player scores points for the bubbles and loses points by eliminating the poor fish.

Try it yourself (control the pufferfish with WASD; no mobile controls, sorry!).

I won’t describe the entire game step by step, but will mention new patterns I introduced there. The full source is on GitHub.

For a game this size, it makes sense to split it into packages. One level of packages should be enough.

game is the entry point, including the Game struct and the initial Donburi world.

component and system packages keep components and systems as described so far.

I like to keep the names singular, so later I get self-explanatory component.Velocity and system.Rendering types.

assets keeps the assets loaded with go:embed for easier distribution. It’s a trivial one in this case, just loading all of them on import. For bigger games, it makes sense to add an asynchronous loader here.

In the engine package, I keep common helper functions that don’t belong anywhere. Things like Timer{}, RandomDuration(), Rect{}, etc. Because they are universal (never specific to the game), it’s easy to copy-paste this package when starting a new game and use them right away.

We’ll get to archetype, domain, and event soon.

The order of imports goes something like this. A package can’t import anything above it.

Donburi comes with the Transform component, which most entities need. It includes the basic data each object in 2D space has: position, rotation, and scale. We no longer need to define them ourselves, as we did in the tiles example.

The 2D vector (math.Vec2) also comes from Donburi, and it’s just a pair of (X, Y) values. I described working with position, rotation, and scale in detail in the previous post.

Working with components can get verbose, so I use a high-level API to simplify it. I keep it in the archetype package.

The API uses the builder pattern. New() creates a new entry with the Transform component, and With() adds more components.

For common objects that can be created in a few places, I also create constructors in the archetype package:

Now, creating a new fish is as simple as:

For some common components like Sprite, I extend the builder so the API is even easier to use. For example, the WithTimeToLive method adds the TimeToLive component and sets its timer to the given duration. It’s easy to extend the API, thanks to keeping it part of the game instead of a generic library.

Transform supports parent-child relationships, which is super handy. When you make an entity a child of another entity, it’s easy to calculate its position, rotation, and scale, taking entities in the hierarchy into account. In other words, you can make it “follow” the parent.

The transform package exposes an API for this:

Have you noticed that Transform uses LocalPosition, LocalRotation, and LocalScale? If the entity has no parent, its local position is the same as its world position. But once it has one, the local position is the position relative to the parent. That’s what the false argument to AppendChild and SetParent controls: with true, Donburi recalculates the local position so the child doesn’t move in the world.

To read the world values, the transform package has functions that return the world position, rotation, and scale. “World” in this context means “Local value plus parent and all grandparents”.

In practice, this means every time we attach an entity as a child to another entity, we only need to worry about setting its local position. All systems using the world position will treat it as being attached to the parent.

We use parent-child relationships when spawning a new bubble. We have a couple of spawner entities in the game world. They are invisible and create new bubbles around them.

When a new bubble appears on a timer, we set its local position:

Because the spawner is set as the parent, we can just get a random distance between -200 and 200, and the bubble will appear within that distance of the spawn point. If we move the spawners, the bubbles will follow them.

The rendering system is more universal now. The key element is the Sprite component, representing an image we draw:

We support layers. The lower layers get drawn first on the screen, so higher layers end up on top. The Order() method makes sprites work with Donburi’s ordered queries, which iterate over entities sorted by layer.

Layers are just arbitrary numbers, but we define a few constants. We’ll have all fish in the background, the player on top of them, and the bubbles above everything else.

We use a single camera that follows the player. We draw the entire game world on the offscreen image in memory. Then, we paint a portion of it onto the actual screen, offset by the camera position.

Rendering text is similar to rendering sprites, but simpler. We use a new component:

We draw entities with this component the same way we draw sprites, but with text instead. This could be improved by extending the component data with things like text color, font size, alignment, etc.

Because of the order of drawers, text will always appear on top of the sprites. For our use case, that’s good enough.

Here’s a comparison of some of the entities and components we use:

Components aren’t just buckets for data, but they should give you a clear idea of what can happen with the entity. Try to find names that clearly describe what the component represents.

We use a similar Velocity system to the one in the previous example.

I wanted to make controls feel a bit like swimming, so there’s also the Drag system. It reduces the velocity of entities with the Drag component over time. This way, after you press a movement button, the player moves for a bit and gradually stops.

Drag also works on other fish, but not on bubbles, which have constant upward velocity. This is an example of how you can control which entities a system handles, and which it doesn’t. Drag is a tag, so it enables or disables the behavior for the chosen entities. We could also dynamically add or remove it.

We use the same mechanism to limit the camera, player, and fish positions, so they never leave the world edges.

For the camera, we adjust the limit based on the screen dimensions:

Note how the limit system works the same for entities as different as the camera and the player, with a slight adjustment of the boundaries. We don’t add the PositionLimit component to the bubbles, because they can escape upwards.

I thought it would be fun to give each fish color a different behavior, like ghosts in Pac-Man:

Each type needs a different state (timers and other data). Instead of using a single component, I decided to go with four, one for each AI type. But there’s still one system. I used a query that combines any of the components:

Four systems would work just as well. I chose a bit less boilerplate.

Bounds is a component that represents the entity’s boundaries in the game world. For example, we use it to check collisions. It’s the entity’s 2D dimensions.

The simplest way is to use the image size as bounds. But we create a separate component to have more control over the dimensions.

We make the bounds a bit smaller than the image. This reduces the collision area. Otherwise, the player would collide with the fish by touching the transparent parts, which would be unintuitive and annoying.

We create a Rect() method that returns a struct filled with the entity’s position together with the bounds, taking scale into account.

Taking scale into account matters because we’ll use different scales for the fish, and the player’s scale will change during gameplay. All logic related to the boundaries needs to consider this.

Calling this method is a bit unusual because of how components work. The BoundsData struct keeps only the dimensions, so we also need to pass the entry to Rect to get the current position.

There’s a trivial Debug system that flips a boolean debug flag. When the flag is on, the rendering system draws the bounds around the sprites.

Donburi supports events. It’s a simple mechanism, as we still have one game loop running. We don’t do any asynchronous processing.

I like working with events because they let you decouple concepts in the game. Many game elements are connected, and over time the logic becomes full of calls to different parts, which is hard to follow.

Let’s consider the Kill system from our game. We look for intersections between a killer (the player object) and a killable (other fish). Once they intersect, we destroy the fish and reduce the player’s points.

The thing is, adding scoring logic here feels beyond the responsibility of this system. It would work just fine, but note how generic the system is now. It doesn’t know anything about fish or the player. It just makes sure that a killer destroys a killable it intersects with.

So we define a Killed event in the event package:

To remove an entity from the world, you can call entry.Remove(). But another system down the stack might still have a leftover reference to it, and then your game will crash. You can check if the entity is valid with entry.Valid(), but it adds a lot of noise to the logic code.

I kept running into this issue over and over, and finally changed the approach.

Instead of removing the entities, we mark them as destroyed with a tag. We can use a helper method:

The Destroy system cleans up the destroyed entities, like a garbage collector. RemoveRecursive also removes all children in the hierarchy.

The order of systems usually doesn’t matter, but here it’s important. Destroy is the last system in the stack, to give other systems a chance to process the entity before it’s removed for good. Note the Remains system, which leaves a skeleton where a fish died. It queries destroyed entities and needs to run before they are removed for good.

For a while, I looked for a good place to keep some of the game’s constants, like the movement speed, initial health points, etc. When you hardcode these values in systems, updating them is annoying.

Similarly, there is often some logic inside systems that’s more related to the inherent game rules than how it works in Ebitengine or Donburi. For example, how some effects stack or how damage is calculated.

I keep this kind of code in the domain package. I took the name from DDD because it felt the most natural to me. The key is that it’s separate, doesn’t import any other game packages, and it’s easy to change and test.

For example, we use the domain rule that “big fish swim slower” in a few spots in the fish AI system. If we wanted to change how it’s calculated, or what else it depends on, we’d change it in one place.

The domain package is a great place for all kinds of testing, since it’s pure logic and doesn’t need the rest of the game engine to work.

You could also build a way to change the domain constants live during gameplay for easier playtesting. Choosing these values is often key to making the game fun to play.

Sometimes, you need a single copy of an object to track data. For example, I keep the screen size and debug toggle in the Settings component. There’s always a single instance of it in the world, and I use a dedicated MustFindSettings() function to get it.

An alternative would be to use a global variable. But I like to stick to the ECS primitives because the world is already passed everywhere, and it’s easy to query what you need from it.

We could also cache these singletons inside systems instead of fetching them every tick. The problems start once you do something unusual, like restarting the level, loading a game, or testing with multiple world instances. I prefer to keep the systems completely stateless, so that the world you pass to Update() keeps the entire game state.

Don’t overuse singletons. We have a single camera and player instance now, but it could take the game in an interesting direction if we added more. ECS works best when you don’t treat the entities as unique snowflakes.

Here’s an example of how the game can change with a few lines of code. Controlling the player works thanks to the Input component. Try adding it to the fish on collision, instead of destroying them:

The fish now start following the player’s moves. But they keep their AI, too, so we need to keep moving to keep them close. Maybe that’s an interesting mechanic? I didn’t plan it beforehand, but I came across it while experimenting with the components. Note we didn’t have to touch the systems at all, because they are generic enough to work with many component configurations.

As much as I like working with ECS, it’s not a silver bullet. It works great in games that simulate many objects with similar behaviors, as we’ve seen so far.

But for many projects, it can feel like too much boilerplate and code scattered with no benefit.

You can’t open the entity’s code and read through its logic, because it’s spread across systems.

It can be difficult to track bugs that happen when systems interact with each other. Not all logic can be captured as an elegant, standalone Update function.

I sometimes choose a hybrid approach for entities that are an exception. A simple Script component with a custom Update function can work fine. I’ll just code the custom logic for the specific entity instead of forcing multiple systems to make it work.

You can also run custom logic in Ebitengine’s Update() and Draw() methods next to the systems. Donburi is easy to plug in where you need it, so you don’t need to go all in. For example, you could keep the game’s UI out of it.

What I described above isn’t an up-front design I made up, but what I ended up with after making games with this architecture and tweaking the approach as I went. Don’t treat it as a definitive guide, but rather as a starting point, and take it from here.

I like how polishing the approach made the next games easier. (Obviously, starting projects is way more fun than finishing them. ð) It freed me from the constant “how to model this?” questions. Instead, I have some familiar ground to start with.

Specifically, it’s easy to copy components and systems between games. Many, like rendering, are universal and can be slightly adjusted, so you never start from zero.

I’m experimenting a lot these days. I also tried making games with agents while keeping the architecture I’m used to. It’s a lot of fun to describe what you have in mind and have quite a polished version in front of you in minutes.

But working this way makes you less involved in the project. As the game gets more complex, you no longer have a clear idea of how everything ties together. That may also be true with old-school typing, but I feel it happens sooner when using AI.

Another downside is that it’s much more tempting to create new features (because it’s so quick) than to polish existing ones and playtest the game so it’s fun to play. Not a big deal if you’re just having fun. But I think there’s value in going through the whole process yourself, although I can’t yet name it precisely.

Gamedev can get ridiculously complex, but many parts work the same way across games. To keep the games built by agents in a familiar structure, I boiled down the approach from my earlier Ebitengine and Donburi games into patterns: Markdown files that agents can follow.

A couple of thoughts before you see the patterns:

You’ll find the files in the patterns directory.

You can find the full source for both games on GitHub.

If you want to see the code for bigger projects, here are some (unfinished ð¥´) games I built with the same approach:

Thanks for reading and have fun making your own games! If you found it useful or would like to read more about some topic, let me know in the comments.

We work on a lot of new useful content. We can let you know when a new post appears. Your e-mail will be safe and not shared with anyone. ðYou will also receive a free "Go With The Domain" e-book!

In the previous post, I looked into running transactions in a layered architecture. Now, let’s consider transactions that need to span more than one service. If you work with microservices, a time may come when you need a transaction running across them. Especially if the way they are split was an afterthought (the unfortunate but likely scenario). Service A calls service B, which calls service C, and if something goes wrong at the end, the system becomes inconsistent.

Here’s a rant I often see in developer communities: I used to love programming because I like building stuff. But my full-time job killed my passion. I spend more time in meetings, fighting over deadlines, and arguing in reviews than working with code. Am I burned out? Is there hope, or do I need a new hobby? Sounds familiar? No wonder we keep looking forward to using a new framework or database â we’re bored.

#9904. Baseten on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

Baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use the latest DeepSeek V4 Flash through Baseten. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to Baseten automatically.

Hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug baseten-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

Important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

We would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49

#9903. Announcing XRAID: declustered parity RAID for zoned XFS

Christoph Hellwig has announced the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS.

The two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...]

Work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it.

The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a new "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems. We have also extended Zonar (The zoned file-system visualisation tool) to show how each logical zone maps onto physical zones on devices.

Hellwig gave a presentation at FOSSY in August on this topic; video of the talk does not seem to be available yet, but his slides are available.

#9900. Janet Reno was talking about my friend Coolio (computer criminal)

AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits.

No, not the rapper Coolio, but rather Dennis M. Moran. No dishonor intended for the real Coolio, the rapper, though arguably mine was harder.

There I was, standing on the couch in my basement, pointing at the TV. Janet Reno is giving a press conference on CNN, vowing to bring these cyber terrorists to justice. My jaw is open, Iâm laughing. I canât believe it. Sheâs talking about my friend Dennis âCoolioâ Moran, a 17-year-old.

We were the #goonies on EFNet. We broke off from #doom, following our friend chunkk, the legendary Doom player (I still havenât seen The Goonies movie though). Some of these people are still very close friends and at the time they were much closer friends than anyone I had IRL since they were computer elite and my local friends were all llamas. Above all, we were still very teenage and very dumb.

They were fond of robotripping, since it was all the drugs teenagers could afford. As a suburban kid from Queens from a loving supportive family I knew drugs were bad and would sit this stuff out. I had a job at a dialup ISP in Manhattan called nyct.net as a FreeBSD sys admin. I was moving up in the world.

Others, not so much. The most extreme robotripper and psychonaut on #goonies was Coolio. He was also a lot of fun. He basically never spoke ill of anyone. Everyone loved him. Girls would fall for him just watching him say stuff on IRC over my shoulder.

He was also the poorest friend Iâve ever had. He grew up in Wolfeboro, New Hampshire. His mom wasnât in his life and his dad was, as far as I knew, a decent fellow, though they struggled to make ends meet and he had lived out of a tent for a period of his life. People mostly sort their friends and they get a picture of the world thatâs very curated. Dennis (and indeed the rest of IRC) was my window out of my Queens NY bubble.

We did eventually hang out IRL. Dennis came to visit me in NYC and we went to Mindless Self Indulgence shows together, which were insanely fun. After one of them the (freakishly tall) lead singer Little Jimmy Urine was offering kisses for $5 (âVD freeâ). Dennis offered $20 over the heads of a bunch of clawing girls and he and Jimmy Urine made out.

When he wasnât talking about drugs or girls, he was talking about hacking. We were all dabbling in computer stuff. We loved Doom and Quake and we had aspirations about becoming game developers. I bought a book on C and installed DJGPP and was trying my best to learn, but lost interest in games and pivoted to networks and coding on Linux. And also hacking. Though it had been out for years, I had just caught up with that Phrack article about Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit and was curious about how to apply it. Dennis was interested too, and we thought about how cool itâd be to write a PoC exploit together.

Dennis found out about a BIND vulnerability with no PoC. We wrote one together. It worked! We were pumped. I thought we should promote internet health by publishing the PoC, since that was how you got people to fix bugs in those days. Dennis goes quiet for a few days. Then he comes back. Bro had been busy, he hacked into all of the vulnerable servers and recruited them into an insane botnet. I was shocked. WTF was he going to do with this? I thought we were just learning and there he goes hacking into half of the DNS servers on the internet! At least he patched BIND for them afterwards.

Dennis reads about the CD Universe extortion attempt and sees a business idea. What if he combines his botnet with smurfing to do massive DDoS attacks? Then he could threaten to knock sites offline if they didnât pay. I thought this sounded crazy but he insisted on trying. His reasoning was you canât just cold email executives out of nowhere and try to extort them. You gotta build up a reputation first. So he flexed his muscle and took down Yahoo!

He would say âwatch thisâ and the sites would go down. First Yahoo, then buy.com and eBay, then etrade.com.

He picked buy.com because it was the day of their IPO. What better way to show his power than ruin a company during the dot com bubble on their IPO day.

In our teenage chat room this all made sense. Like a lot of teenagers (and adults), Dennis thought wealth was often illegitimately acquired, and that it was only fair to take from the rich in the bullshit days of the dot com bubble. Thug life, kind of. Definitely worked on the girls, which was probably not healthy for him.

To learn more about his views on wealth maybe we should go back to Wolfeboro. I visited twice, once while he was in jail and once just to hang out and party, and it was absolutely nothing like where I was from in Queens. According to Google itâs a small town of 6,000 known as being full of lakefront summer homes. The part I saw was very much not summer homes. It was houses in the sticks. The rich, such as Mitt Romney, were vacationing in his town while his family was, at times, living in a tent.

Which brings us back to the basement. Iâm standing on the couch, pointing at Janet Reno on the TV, laughing. She says theyâll find whoever did this. I know who did this. I know what he used, too, because I helped write it. Are we all going to jail??

Dennis wasnât done though. He had previously rooted DNS servers and defaced dare.com and cwc.gov, but took the opportunity to deface rsa.com after the DDoS attacks. He did recruit his friends on IRC to help him write ad copy for the defacements. I am sad to admit some of those are my words.

He was especially tickled by defacing RSA since they had just put out a press release advertising that they could help defend against his DDoS attacks. Rekt.

This played out over the course of a couple of days. Being teenagers on IRC, we didnât exactly all keep his secret.

We were âinfiltratedâ by an assistant security officer at Stanford named David Brumley. He came on calling himself âaforceâ and he reeked of How Do You Do Fellow Kids energy, but it still took us way too long to kick him out. It was all for naught anyway: he was tapping the ircd at Stanford, an EFNet server, and could read absolutely everything, private messages included. Coming into the channel was probably just to provoke us into revealing even more. Oh, uh, it also didnât help that Dennisâs RSA defacement specifically taunted aforce, which directly linked someone in #goonies to the crime.

Once word got out that US digital infrastructure was being brought to its knees by a robotripping 17-year-old, the intensity died down. They ultimately did arrest Dennis, and showed him a thick stack of IRC logs of teenagers bullshitting, which is as hilarious as it sounds. He admitted to defacing the web sites, and to getting into Army and Air Force computers at four military bases, but denied launching the DDoS attacks.

As it turned out, we were not all going to jail. Nothing happened to me. No FBI visit. No emails from third parties. Nothing. It was as if I had never been in the room.

Meanwhile, in Canada, a copycat named Mafiaboy took credit for all of them. Iâm not saying he did none of them. Dennis didnât launch DDoS attacks against news sites since he thought they would help spread the story about his underworld reputation. So, itâs possible Mafiaboy did do those. No dishonor intended for Mafiaboy either. Iâm sure he was a legit cyber criminal in his own way.

Dennis didnât exactly get off scot-free. He was sentenced to a year in county jail and was released after nine months. He was also ordered to pay $15,000 in restitution, $5,000 of it to RSA. A security company collecting damages for getting hacked. IMO that situation is a wash.

When I visited him in jail, the Carroll County House of Corrections, I was expecting him to be depressed but he seemed really upbeat about it. He was almost having fun. He was treating it like a sleepaway camp, and the other inmates seemed to love him. While we were talking I overheard an extremely loud, very powerful toilet flush. He said something nuts like âOh, yeah. Some kid joined our block the other day. We tried to flush him down that toilet but he wouldnât fit so we decided he was cool.â (Years later he would tell me another story, this time about prison. Dennis was a not-big white guy, and a very large black man who had just moved to his cell wrapped a towel around his head and yanked it so hard that Dennis flipped off the bed and hit the ground. Terrifying. Dennis got up laughing his ass off, and the guy ended up being his best friend in there.)

And donât just take it from his IRC friends that he was lovable. Paul Zimmerman, a local businessman who wrote to Dennis in jail and then visited him there, told a reporter in 2001: âI found him to be a most delightful person.â And: âHe was not angry or vindictive or mad at the system. He was taking his licks in an honorable way.â

Anyway, at that age you donât usually get such an early view of law enforcement, but here it was: they didnât really care about the truth of the story. They knew full well Dennis did it. The stack of IRC logs printed out screamed that he did it. The FBI has them. They know. But Mafiaboy was already willing to take the rap so why bother indicting Dennis.

Dennisâs story has not fully been told to this day because he did not have a rehabilitation arc. He didnât turn it into a career the way Mafiaboy did. Not because he never had chances: Dennis was offered a security engineering gig at a local firm but one day just walked off the job, bored.

The years after that went in cycles. Heâd get straight and hold down an honest job in a sandwich shop for a year or two. Then heâd lose touch with reality and do some nonsensical crime. Heâd sober up in jail, which he seemed not too upset about, and then heâd be back to normal.

One time he dropped LSD and started going through peopleâs mailboxes. He was convicted of that. Soon after starting his jail sentence he came on IRC, and he told us he had secured work release, helping a local strip club with their web site. Doing his time meant heâd leave jail, go to the strip club, hang out with strippers and smoke weed, then go back to his cell in jail at night. When society needed Dennis to repay his debts this is usually what it had in mind.

He spent a while bouncing around the country. He had lots of friends from IRC who welcomed him into their homes, often romantically. Ultimately he settled in the Bay Area.

I wish the story ended there. We thought heâd eventually figure it out.

This story is a secret weâve been keeping for Dennis all of this time: he did launch those DDoS attacks, and we watched him do it. Thereâs really no need anymore. Dennis had a secret of his own: he was addicted to heroin, and he hid that from us for years. It seems he found a community of heroin addicts out there, and it got out of control.

I have some guilt about all this. Dennis went to jail, which is probably where he learned about heroin. A few of the rest of us on IRC got questioned in person by the FBI. Absolutely nothing happened to me.

I really loved Dennis. We all did. We tried to help Dennis but couldnât. He threatened to kill himself if we ever said the word ârehabâ around him. He dabbled in dealing research chemicals in the Bay Area, and on the darkweb for Bitcoin, but was eventually busted and the walls began to close in around him as his court date loomed. He became paranoid and started lashing out. He was using all of the time. The last thing that happened between us was that I joined a different chat room I knew he was in. It was on a different platform, so I picked a different nick, as a joke, but one I thought he would easily grok as me. He didnât recognize the nick and freaked out. He accused me of being a narc. I told him I was sorry and that I wasnât trying to stress him out, but he just quit in a huff. I never talked to him again. He disappeared from IRC for several weeks. I ended up hearing from mutual IRC friends that he had been found dead in his room, in 2013 of a heroin overdose. Age 30.

There was never a proper goodbye. On some level I still donât accept that heâs gone.

I still have dreams sometimes where Coolio connects to IRC and joins the chat, and we all shoot the shit like nothing had ever happened.

Did you know Coolio? Did he DDoS attack you? :P Letâs talk about it on X, Bluesky, Mastodon or Hacker News.

#9899. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

For a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

You can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Finally, let’s get Muse Glimmer to do some light RSI. We can instruct our agent to optimize its own inference engine for specific hardware, in this case a Nvidia H100. To do this, the agent will need to use another inference engine, like Inference Endpoints above.

Muse Glimmer benchmarks its own single-H100 serving stack, testing one reversible change at a time while holding the workload fixed. It keeps only correctness-passing gains and finishes with the fastest reproducible configuration. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/onyx-optimization-progress.gif?download=true

Try Muse Glimmer as a Hugging Face research agent. The Gradio Space sends each model request to a private Hugging Face Inference Endpoint through its OpenAI-compatible API. It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

#9897. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss
