InfoQ Homepage Articles Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility

Nov 16, 2026 18 min read

Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.

Application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals quickly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.

Agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

This article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.

The model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.

Some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it quickly is part of the architecture.

A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.

The recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.

This is especially important in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.

The architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.

Figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author)

The organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.

Figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author)

In the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.

A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.

This distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.

The reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.

MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.

The "one place" property is important. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.

Figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author)

The pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.

The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.

Table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view

The reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.

The Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.

The Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.

Figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author)

All agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.

The quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.

In practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.

A common event contract is just as important as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.

The simplified example below shows a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.

Consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.

The ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.

Retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.

Suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.

When an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.

The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.

Prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.

The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.

The important design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.

False positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.

Human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.

The platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.

Table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements

This is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.

The policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.

Figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author)

Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.

The gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.

Typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.

Content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.

For regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.

Teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.

Teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.

Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.

The compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.

Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.

In regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.

We expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.

Table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements

Agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:

The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.

Frank Vandermeiren has announced the creation of the Manjaro Project e.V., a nonprofit organization in Germany that is independent of the Manjaro GmbH & Co KG company. This is following a governance struggle that took place earlier this year between a number of Manjaro Linux contributors and Philip Müller, project lead and CEO of the Manjaro company.

At the moment, we are still working on optimizing the new development infrastructure, which was partly necessitated by the ongoing (A.I.) bot attacks against our old infrastructure.

#9894. [$] A new generation of futexes

Futexes are a kernel subsystem that provides support for fast mutexes in user space. While futexes can indeed be fast, they are not fast enough for a number of users. Partly as a result of that, the implementation of futexes has grown in complexity over the years, with two basic variants on offer. The desire for faster futexes remains, though, and that inspires new patches, including this series from Suleiman Souhlal adding a third futex class called "futex PING" for "priority inheritance next generation".

#9893. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#9892. On Leaving Swift for Rust

Yesterday I resigned from the Swift Android workgroup. I’ve received a number of inquiries about this, and rather than responding individually to each one, I figured I would just write up a post with my reasoning and submit it to the public record.

First off, my resignation was not triggered by any sort of conflict, grievance, or specific incident. Early Swift community efforts got off to a rough start when Swift language creator Chris Lattner quit due to what he described as a “toxic environment”. This event predates my direct involvement in the project, so I am not privy to the specifics. But I want to be clear that this was in no way my experience: everyone I interacted with, both from Apple and external organizations, both in meetings and in forum discussions and direct messages, have been polite, courteous, and the paragon of civility and professional conduct. Despite Apple having an ancient blood feud with Android, and my own rather acrimonious relationship with certain divisions of the company, every single one of my direct interactions with the Swift team has been pleasant and productive. I will miss our meeting and chats, and I harbor zero ill-will towards the project or any of the individual members I’ve worked with.

By way of background, I’ve been programming for over 40 years. I started with Basic, then Pascal, on to C, then C++, over to Java, up to Scala, back down to Kotlin, around to Objective-C, before finally landing on Swift. Swift is a delightful language: I loved it from day one and I’ve been boosting it around the world since 2014. Swift really “does what it says on the tin”: it couples the performance of C++ with the ease of Java. And Swift is as developer-friendly as it gets: an intuitive object-oriented syntax coupled with maximally efficient value types, fabulous tooling (on Apple platforms), and a thoughtfully-designed build system.

I have not soured on Swift: I think it is an excellent language, and it is here to stay. But it is here to stay in that same straight-and-narrow lane shared by all corporate-directed languages, like C# is here to stay for Microsofties and like Kotlin is here to stay for Androidophiles. Which isn’t bad in and of itself: if you want to write software solely for [CORPORATE PRODUCT], then [CORPORATE LANGUAGE] will always be well-maintained, supported, and they will always provide support for their latest products, with an easy migration path forward. They are the safe and happy path, as long as you stay in your lane and limit your ambitions to writing software for [CORPORATE PRODUCT].

But when you stray from that happy path, the rough edges start surfacing, and there is no one getting a paycheck to smooth those out. Swift for Android/Windows/other-non-Apple-platform is in exactly that position: yes, it technically works, and yes, the language steering committees are committed to continuing the level of support they promised, but it will never be the same seamless experience as developing for iOS/watchOS/visionOS/whateverOS. This extends beyond the language and into the tooling: Skip enables you use Xcode to develop your apps in parallel for iOS and Android, but this has only been achieved in the face of Xcode’s constitutional hostility towards doing anything other than optimizing for their own first-party platforms.

If humanity were destined to continue creating software solely with their monkey brains and meat fingers, Swift would likely be the language I would have stuck with until the day I retired. But that isn’t the trajectory we are currently on. Barring such speculative calamities as “model collapse”, Butlerian Jihad, or Skynet, we have taken a turn in a new direction.

We software developers have collectively [as/de]cended to a plane where we now direct the computers to write our computer code, and these computers have decided that they really prefer computery languages over the humany languages. Humany languages are those designed to fit inside our wonderful little biological brains. I have grave reservations about all of this from many perspectives: ethical, ecological, political, socio-economical (just to name a few). But it is what it is, and all but the most ardent of refusenik software developers have come around to this view in the past 6—12 months.

Swift isn’t a computery language, it is a developer-friendly humany language: it is a better Java, a better C#, and a (much) better Objective-C. Throughout my career I’ve been able to accomplish amazing feats in these languages, disproportionate to my limited intellect and abilities, but that comes at the cost of these languages being hobbled in pursuit of their mission to slice and dice complex problems in such a way as to be tractable for one or more human brains. I speak of object-orientation; I speak of automatic memory management.

But there is one very computery language that until recently has been waiting in the wings…

In February, Andreas Kling dropped Swift for Rust for the Ladybird browser, a 180°1 turnabout from their opposite decision from a year earlier. In July, Jarred Sumner ported Bun from Zig to Rust. In September, David Heinemeier Hansson filicided Ruby on Rails for Rust. And this trend is only accelerating: nearly every week there is some new project converting some massively complex codebase from language X to Rust. PostgreSQL! The TypeScript compiler! These projects are coming fast and furious with no sign of slowing down. And for every one of these projects, over 95% of the code was not written by a human.

Swift is wonderful. It enabled me to bring iOS development to Android through Skip and share a single codebase between the two dominant mobile platforms. LLMs are quite proficient with Skip: Claude or Codex can one-shot a passable prototype for a new iOS+Android app written in Swift in a matter of minutes and you can have it running side-by-side on emulators or devices and start iterating to your heart’s content. The single shared codebase gives the LLMs the ability to develop and refine features in single codebase, rather than constantly needing one codebase (e.g., in Kotlin and Compose) play catch-up with the other (Swift and SwiftUI) codebase.

But I always wanted more from Skip. I wanted to add support for desktop platforms for Mac, Linux, and Windows. I wanted the same codebase to run on the web through webassembly. I wanted to build for emerging mobile platforms like HarmonyOS and anything that might come next. And I wanted to do it all using each platform’s native first-party toolkits rather than the usual web-shell compromise or pixel-painting mimicry, because, like Apple, I believe that the best apps are built with native SDKs.

In addition to supporting a wider range of target platforms, I also wanted to bring this power to more development host platforms. You can currently only use Skip to develop apps from a macOS host; Windows and Linux users are left out in the cold. And while there is some impressive work happening to bring iOS development to non-macOS hosts, those tools will take a while to percolate, and appear to face the wrath of the platform overlords. For Skip, it is irksome enough that even the Android target of the app cannot be developed on a non-macOS host, but when it comes to expanding the platform targets, it becomes downright absurd if, say, you would be unable use Skip to develop a HarmonyOS app from a Windows host.

Swift — both the language as well as the tooling — is simply not equipped to handle those needs yet, and despite its impressive progress with their cross-compilation SDKs, I don’t think it ever will be. It will always be an Apple-platforms-first technology, and anything beyond that insular world will be consigned to an eternal Sisyphean uphill grind.

Rust, on the other hand, wasn’t designed for a single platform, or even a small handful of platforms. They support 300 platforms. Cross-compilation has been a foundational principle from day one, rather than being a bolted-on afterthought. This leads to an ecosystem that values building for everything and everyone, with no platform bias. When I started out on this journey, I was frankly astonished when the code I was tinkering with for iOS — which included dozens of rando crates.io dependencies that I yolo’d into my little research project — just worked for Android. And Windows. And Linux. And HarmonyOS. And Webassembly.

But getting back to the point: Swift will be fine. It is here to stay, at least for Apple platform development. And Skip will be fine: it has a growing community of developers and maintainers that will keep the project going strong and keep up with Swift and Xcode updates. Skip will continue to improve the Android side of the coin in step with Apple’s improvement of the iOS side. I am confident that both technologies will keep chugging along indefinitely, powering fabulous apps on Apple and Android platforms alike, well into the future.

But that is not my future. Software development is suddenly no longer hard. App development is suddenly no longer hard. And I need to be solving hard problems in order to thrive.

The initial revision of this post said “360°” when it meant “180°”. Thank you, internet commentariat, for your gracious corrections. ↩

#9890. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.)

Both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

DeepSeek-V3.2 — by difficulty (baseline → +memory): the two systems start from different no-memory baselines (79.8 vs 72.0 TGC overall) because of the prompt-template difference above.

#9889. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#9886. [$] Zellij manages terminal workspaces with style

Zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

#9885. What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

Questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully."

Note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

What has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:

Participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:

51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:

35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:

The paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

An evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

We have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a new arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗

The most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:

Pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

Some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics said "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check."

So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

To the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

Stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗

One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.

The scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days shows how quickly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻

What I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊

The point about reviewing capacity is particularly important... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️

Most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨

#9884. Redict deprecated in favor of Valkey

Drew DeVault has announced that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

We recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.
