Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will talk about the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and query builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you avoid falling into generic type gymnastics and monomorphization bloat? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.

Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Does this idea still hold up when you bring it into a real, more complex project?When building my own Rust ORM, Kova, I applied this pattern across the entire type system. It is a good concrete example of how this plays out in practice.ORMs are where the Orphan Rule hurts the most. A single table often mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types. Kova's core Encode and Decode traits use the exact generic slot design we just walked through:pub trait Encode<'a, X = ()> { fn encode(self) -> Result>; } pub trait Decode: Sized { fn decode(value: Value<'_>) -> Result; }Because Kova hands the extension point to the user, it only needs built-in support for basic database primitives: integers, floats, booleans, strings, and byte arrays. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will talk about the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and query builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you avoid falling into generic type gymnastics and monomorphization bloat? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.

It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will talk about the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and query builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you avoid falling into generic type gymnastics and monomorphization bloat? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.

#9830. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9829. Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Last month, Microsoft disclosed a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, but messaging regarding a patch was unclear.

Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.

According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.

The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."

A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extension to Third-Party Breach

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.

CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.

As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.

The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."

But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability.

"Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."

Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9828. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9827. CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

New questionnaire captures critical data and information that improves the agency’s ability to assess incidents, identify trends and prioritize response actions.

WASHINGTON — Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.

The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”

While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.

For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questionsweb page.

As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.

#9826. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

InfoQ Homepage News Production AI, Architecture Trade-offs & Team Design: InfoQ Opens Registration for 6 January Cohorts

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read

InfoQ has opened registration for six online cohort workshops starting between January 9 and 22, 2027. Covering AI Engineering, Software Architecture, and High-Performing Teams, the five-week programs bring senior engineers, architects, and engineering leaders together to work through technical and organizational decisions with experienced practitioners.

The workshops go beyond studying technical material. Participants apply frameworks from QCon and InfoQ to decisions from their own work, compare approaches with practitioners from other organizations, and return to discuss what they tried and learned. Working across different organizational contexts helps expose trade-offs and assumptions that may not emerge from an internal discussion alone.

Each cohort combines four hours of live facilitated sessions per week, independent application work, and a program-specific capstone.

Production AI involves decisions beyond model selection: how context is retrieved and maintained, how much autonomy agents should have, and how reliability, latency, and inference costs are managed.

The InfoQ AI Engineering Program examines these decisions through RAG architectures, agent design, platforms, and evaluation. Participants work through technical approaches and failure modes, applying them to AI systems or proposals from their own work.

Architecture choices are shaped by system requirements, team boundaries, platform ownership, and organizational constraints.

The InfoQ Architect Program covers distributed systems, decentralized decisions, platform engineering, and AI architecture. Participants apply the material to architecture decisions they currently own, compare trade-offs with peers, and practice communicating their reasoning to stakeholders.

The capstone involves co-authoring a technical article examining AI's role in software architecture or platform engineering. Selected articles may be published on InfoQ.

Both cohorts start January 22 and are facilitated by Luca Mezzalira, independent software architect and author of Building Micro-Frontends. Friday sessions are offered at 09:30 GMT and 10:00 EST.

Faster coding does not necessarily improve delivery when reviews, approvals, or infrastructure dependencies become the constraint. AI agents also change how responsibilities are divided and which work requires human judgment.

The InfoQ High-Performing Teams Program examines team structure, ownership, delivery flow, AI responsibilities, and engineering metrics as one operating model.

Participants evaluate constraints in their own team environments, compare approaches with peers, and develop a proposed target operating model covering responsibilities, workflow, and measurement.

The January 12 cohort is facilitated by Olimpiu Pop, InfoQ Podcast co-host with experience in solutions architecture, engineering management, and CTO roles. Sessions run on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from 16:00 to 18:00 CET.

The live online workshops focus on discussion and application rather than recorded lectures. Participants work with an experienced facilitator and a small cross-company peer group, bringing current engineering decisions into the sessions and testing approaches between meetings.

Sessions are not recorded, allowing participants to discuss organizational constraints more openly. Certification requires attendance, active participation, and successful completion of the program capstone.

Participation costs USD 1,470 per person. Full schedules, syllabi, and registration details are available on the InfoQ Online Certification Programs website.

#9824. People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 22: You can love AI without being blind to the cybersecurity risks. The tendency for humans to anthropomorphize the conversations and interactions we're having with AI is growing into potential delusion.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello everyone, and welcome back to Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I am so excited to introduce our guest, Jaya Baloo, who is currently CISO and COO of Aisle. Welcome. Thank you so much for joining us, Jaya.

Jaya Baloo: Thank you so much for inviting me, Becky. Thank you.

DR's Becky Bracken: We are thrilled you're here. I want to explain to our audience a little bit about why I am so particularly excited to have you here. Recently, I was in the audience at ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, and Jaya gave what I just thought was a blockbuster talk about sort of merging AI and quantum, and it was fascinating. There's a specific chunk of her talk that I invited her to talk about today. And it's something I'm just calling: Why is everyone so weird about AI?

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

And so, it stuck with me for days afterward. I kept having the conversation with people because, as I was just explaining to Jaya, we hear people talk about this on the edges, but I hadn't heard a technologist and an expert explain it so plainly, which I think Jaya is also sort of your superpower. But just in the past couple of days, we have Sam Altman who came out saying no one needs their own RAM. They're calling him "RAM Altman." I mean, it's just that people are weird. So, can you explain to me why you dropped that section in, and do you know why it stuck with me for so long? Why is it hitting so close?

Jaya Baloo: I think it's because for ages, when we looked at AI, we had this notion of the uncanny valley, you know? Like, at what point is it so convincing to me that I think I'm speaking to a human? And I think it's clear to say we've passed this uncanny valley. We're fully, you know, believing the conversations that we're having with AI. They could be coming from another human. So, the tendency for us to anthropomorphize the conversations, the interactions that we're having with AI is growing and growing.

And you see people who are not just having a sort of delusional psychosis sometimes of aggrandizement of their own intellect when talking to AI and convinced because of some of the sick fancy that's built into AI that they're super intelligent or their ideas are incredibly unique and creative, or that they're actually the ones to save humanity. You know, I think that the problems that we see with people who are potentially susceptible to that are just made much worse by the current evolution and this current state of AI that we have today. It's just so real. It's so convincing. And we then tend to make it more human.

Related:NIST Finalizes Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance, GAO Offers a Reality Check

DR's Becky Bracken: So, let's go through some of the examples that you gave in your talk. One of them that made me cackle out loud was when you were playing video of a robot doing kung fu with a caption: Why can't we teach it to do laundry? Explain that example for us.

Jaya Baloo: Yeah, so really what I'm talking about is that, you know, we already have a whole bunch of threats right now when we're dealing with AI. And that's really about AI's capability to both uncover vulnerabilities as well as having vulnerabilities in and of itself. So, AI as a potential for insider threat. As we already have these problems, both in our legacy tech debt and in the new technology that we're building with AI, we have more problems.

Now, I have no idea who thought this was a great idea to take these things that are entrenched with these problems, and put it into something that can actually cause physical harm and teach a robot, which by the way, I should be clear, this was the Unitree humanoid robot. It was announced a little bit over a week ago. But let's say that it was announced at the end of October. And this robot was demonstrated on YouTube to do all this cool kung fu stuff.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

And the issue with this that I have is that this can cause actual physical harm. What is it actually bringing humans in terms of value? And honestly, I would be much happier with a humanoid robot that can do the wash, fold the laundry, and sort it out in the kid's hamper. That would be helpful. It wouldn't be something where I'd be terrified to have this thing anywhere near us. And I think that this is something that I feel is genuinely problematic. Just because you can doesn't mean you should when it comes to some of these implementations. And if you cannot get the security right, don't exacerbate and increase the potential for doing damage and harm to humans.

I feel like we forgot that as we're building. You know, we need to solve tech debt, we need to make sure that we have secure-by-default systems, and then you can implement it in something that coexists with us in the physical realm. So that was my point about that. But I really want to say the real issue here is that Unitree had not one, but two, remote backdoors in its quadruped robots. There are multiple security issues with its humanoid robots. And I think knowing that you can remotely take over these robots, and again, like they're capable of physical harm, I think that we really need to rethink and really considerately position these types of devices in light of things like the Cyber Resilience Act.

You know, should we allow hardware and software manufacturers to bring out this kind of technology with the potential risk that it poses? And not just from a cyber perspective, but from a physical one as well.

DR's Becky Bracken: What were some of your other top examples of what's another one that you'd like to highlight here of people being kind of weird about AI?

Jaya Baloo: Well, so I think a slide that you may have initially seen is, and I kind of didn't want to reference it right away in my first answer, was about the fact that we're getting strained in terms of the religiousness around AI. That we both have this tendency to first say, actually, you know, maybe they're sentient, which Anthropic has been talking about in the Vatican with different religious leaders trying to talk about the potential consciousness of AI.

And although I love science fiction, I love it, I just feel, are we really there yet? Are we there, or is this a marketing ploy? What is this? And I'm genuinely trying to understand because it polemicizes what should be a very rational debate into two camps. Those who believe, like already now, we're at the point of talking about consciousness and sentience of these AI systems.

And then the other camp, which actually rebukes AI in the name of Jesus. And I think that was the slide that people also laughed at the conference about. But this is real. And I find it bizarre that we have these phenomena happening and that we don't fully understand the societal consequences either of introducing these systems, which again, let's talk about what they are. They're a bunch of graphics cards in a data center running software.

I am a full Kool-Aid drinker of the notion of complexity and emergence and understanding that even though with a relative set of simple ingredients you have potentially complex outcomes. Drank that Kool-Aid long ago. I believe in this stuff, but I just don't think we're there yet.

So, I feel this has a sort of reductionism effect for the debate that we should be having over how do we do responsible AI by pulling it into these two polemic camps.

DR's Becky Bracken: You also tied it to a lot of end-of-times cult-like thinking, but it does raise the question, which you sort of alluded to a moment ago, how much of this is being driven by marketing of these frontier models, of the [Sam] Altmans of the world, of the Peter Thiels of the world who are out talking. How much of a receptive audience are they finding in the cybersecurity sector, do you think? I mean, is that the primary dynamic at play?

Jaya Baloo: Well, look, I think that we need to separate what is actually happening, which is we do have a bunch of vulnerability discoveries that are happening because of AI. We do have automation for real. It is genuinely happening. We do have automation of these hacking frameworks from Strix, RTec-Ai, Cairn. We are seeing hacking frameworks that are actually in RTec specifically, that are actually being used in real-world hacks. So I'm not trying to discount the facts.

However, what I'm urging to do is the call that, for example, Ciaran Martin, the former head of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), always makes, which is, "Calm the FUD down."

And the fear, uncertainty, doubt that we're introducing here is not helpful. And the reason that I find it really unhelpful is because we know to a large extent how we should perform some sort of containment in terms of egress filtering and sandboxing of these systems.

They may not be perfect, but we've always worked with this notion of defense in depth: assume that one measure fails and that you have additional countermeasures to prevent an actual collapse of the security of the system. I think that that is something that we are actually forgetting right now. And I think it's really important to say, OK, what are the things we genuinely need that would be considered helpful innovation for this? And I think that what we're missing is a lot of the observability here around these AI systems.

So, for example, if we're trying to understand how these systems have potentially been poisoned or Trojanized inherently, then the ability to actually understand how that training data has been populated, even when you only have open-weight models, that would be helpful.

Another thing is additional understanding around this notion of J-space (Jacobian space). So, agent intent. If you know that you have a human operator that brings their own intent to the mix, you know and understand that an AI system might have capabilities and intent that diverge from that human operator, you need to understand when and where that first point of evidence for collecting that divergence could be. We're not there yet either.

So, I would like us to focus on those things rather than the FUD, like Ciaran Martin and a bunch of other renowned cybersecurity people have been saying for a while, like we really need to focus on the things that are breaking.

And really need to focus on the things that we need to be building rather than everyone up in arms about this "Vulnpocalypse," "Breachpocalypse," etc. Apocalypses that are predicted.

DR's Becky Bracken: What is the best way to push back against this sort of rampant anthropomorphization of these agents? You know, I mean, even when researchers are using words like they will "cheat," which assumes that there is a moral compass there to begin with. But at the same time, the goal is for them to be as human as possible? How do we thread that needle?

Jaya Baloo: "They will cheat" is the reward hacking notion that this is a utility that is trying to find the shortest path to success. That means that things that a human would consider part of that moral compass, not to cheat, not to lie, not to evade, etc., that we are projecting this somehow on these AI systems and assuming that the guardrails that we've put in place will cover it.

But I don't think that you can make that assumption clearly, because I don't think we're always in the position to inspect all of the guardrails and know when they've been appropriately applied. And so, I think that there's also this issue of finiteness. Can you have a finite set of guardrails that are actually encompassing the kinds of things that you want to do? And I think the answer to that is probably not.

You know, you’re probably still going to have a few things that escape your potential for, like having this perfectly constructed set of guardrails. Those are like mathematical limitations.

What I would love to encourage us to do is genuinely try to understand better the types of technology that we put into our networks, give access to our data, give a single API token and say "YOLO" to our enterprises, because I don't think we have this under control. And I think that's the real worry that I have.

If we don't understand fully and we're not aware of all of the potential risks, for example, cheating or lying, misrepresentation, etc., if we don't understand that, then we certainly can't have all of these elevated privileges and permissions that we're doing. I think this was the point I was trying to make about when you have capability, you need to kind of always have this subset of this accountability and authorization that you're giving something. And right now, we forgot that lesson. You know, we said, here's all the stuff that you've got access to. You go. And I really feel like we need to rewind a little bit just this part. And that requires better understanding of what they're capable of in terms of the risks.

DR's Becky Bracken: So, what is the next step forward? If you had your team and you were seeing some of this sort of extreme thinking, you know, seeping into your defense planning, what would you say to them? What is the correct reset function here?

Jaya Baloo: I'm really worried about the fact that we are genuinely at risk of losing some of the critical thinking when we're applying AI systems. And you see that already with our coding practices; we are allowing more and more of that initial thinking. So, planning our projects, actually executing the code, reviewing that code, proving it, etc.

DR's Becky Bracken: Which is shocking in such an evidence-based field. You know, it is shocking that it's gone so fast. Am I right?

Jaya Baloo: I feel like we kind of learned this lesson in security in the past too. So it's kind of like, Back to the Future, as well. Every time we tell people about "you should do this because it's secure," if it's not an easy or fun thing to do, you know people won't do it, right? The utility surpasses the convenience. All of the brain elements that would constitute your frontal lobe warning you for this risk. Like, we just lose it. We become teenagers again. Our risk level and tolerance are high. We are happy to take these risks if it makes our life a little bit easier. And I think we shouldn't forget that.

So, AI as an assistant is an incredibly powerful, incredibly useful tool. And especially when we're trying to drive efficiencies with all this technology and all this cost. And you're talking about, you know, "RAM Altman." I think the accessibility of AI and the sovereignty of it is not something we should be taking for granted. And it absolutely is a problem.

So, knowing all of this, you know, the drive to get this convenience, to get this utility, to get this thing available, that is so overcoming any type of hesitation we would have, like, "Is this safe? Should I really use this?" "Will I get dumber if I keep doing this all the time and outsource my thinking?" And I think that's where we actually still need to keep in mind this notion of: What are we giving up to get this utility?

DR's Becky Bracken: Maybe that's why what you were saying hit so hard because I haven't heard a lot of technologists take that position. You know much better than I do, but they are all gas, no breaks, whatever it takes, let's just not lose the wave. And this return to critical thinking, it seems new. Among your peers and colleagues, do you hear the same kind of concern about losing critical thinking?

Jaya Baloo: I think this is the problem with the Kool-Aid. I think at Aisle we certainly have that. I think there's a strong tendency amongst security professionals, but also AI professionals. So, my co-founder, Stanislav Fort, who is amazing, has always kind of thought about AI safety and interpretability. And he has been the person to say, for example, we initially set up Aisle to do vulnerability remediation. And you can imagine that as a CISO, I was like, all right, if we can do this and we can do this well, let's just remediate all the things. Let's just give it access. And he has always urged caution, always urged caution to say, "You know what? We're not there yet"

Unless we can fully confidently trust the AI to make those changes, I always want a human approving the PRs to any code request. I just don't think that what we have in our co-founder is a universal quality in all AI companies. So, I think that like my other co-founder, Ondřej Vlček, who is CISO for multiple companies, including Avast. We have this tendency because we've been burned. So we are, you know, a once-burned, twice-shy kind of notion.

We really think about this from a security-oriented risk-mitigation perspective while actually wanting. I have to be very honest with you, I love AI. But that love shouldn't be blind. It should take the appropriate measure of what is it that I love? And why do I love it? And, you know, what is the benefit to humanity? And Becky, there's a story that I didn't tell on stage.

There are so many good things we can do with AI, but the one thing that I'm the most encouraged of is ... have you heard about the story with the guy and the dog in Australia?

DR's Becky Bracken: No, I don't think I have.

Jaya Baloo: So, this was a machine learning engineer whose dog developed cancer, inoperable, and the dog had to be put down, was the diagnosis. And what he then did is sequence the dog's DNA. You know, this is a guy with no biology background, sequenced the dog's DNA, and figured out what was wrong in the DNA that caused the cancer, developed an mRNA vaccine with AlphaFold.

The most expensive part of the experiment apparently was to actually synthesize the vaccine. And then he administered it to his dog; he had to get permission for that. And Rosie's tumors shrank, and she's is still here and is still hanging out and playing ball with this machine learning engineer.

So I love this story, and this is why I love AI. Because I think if it can unlock the potential benefits, that is amazing. I want those benefits. I just want to make sure that we minimize the downside risks that are inevitable with this kind of technology. And we just need to figure out how we do that. So, we shouldn't go screaming into the abyss, like, yay! You know, I don't want us to be a bunch of lemmings following AI down the abyss.

I just want us to manage that risk and take the benefits while eyes wide open, understanding that right now we need to make sure that we do have enough RAM, you know, and that we do have sovereign compute, that we do not sacrifice all our clean water

DR's Becky Bracken: No one has to give up their computer for OpenAI?

Jaya Baloo: Yeah. I think the future of AI is probably more decentralized than the frontier labs have us think right now.

DR’s Becky Bracken: How much of this is being driven by investment dollars and hyping up stock price? Because we talked around in our editorial meeting about well, is this just a collective psychosis issue? And it's like, well, first, let's be careful about saying "psychosis," but also are we being marketed into a psychosis?

Jaya Baloo: I would love to have a balanced approach. I'm not saying that there's no marketing being done. I think that is certainly being done. I don't think we should eliminate that. I think it would be naive to assume otherwise. At the same time, going full tilt that it's all just marketing is the wrong approach. I think two things can be true at the same time. And I want us to consider this more nuanced thing. And I really want our brains to hold the capacity that both things are true.

There is absolutely a marketing effort. OK, when you have these kinds of companies going to IPO and it's not just OpenAI, it's also Anthropic, and it's also probably a whole bunch of other, you know, parts of this wheel that are actually driving this rage. But there are genuinely risks that we must counter. So, I really do worry about that. And I don't think that that is psychosis.

You must have seen the filing of Anthropic for the IPO. And one of those things that is in that document is there's a very real existential threat that AI could kill us all. I think that's maybe the first time that was ever put into a filing of a company potentially going to IPO. And even there, I think, surely that is not marketing. Surely there are intelligent, thoughtful humans that want to warn of a potential risk that they genuinely see for themselves. I think we need to evaluate the difference between that and how much space there is between the marketing and the genuine risk. But I do think there is a genuine risk. There is. And we shouldn't downplay it as psychosis, while at the same time recognize that there's marketing.

DR's Becky Bracken: I want to thank you so much for coming. You've given me a whole other set of things to think about. Thank you for sharing your deep expertise and your thoughts with us today. We really appreciate it.

Jaya Baloo: No worries, thank you for having me.

DR's Becky Bracken: This has been Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken. Thank you so much for joining us. We'll see you next time.

The Dark Reading Editorial Team consists of Kelly Jackson Higgins, Fahmida Y Rashid, Tara Seals, Rob Wright, Becky Bracken, Alex Culafi, Arielle Waldman, and Kristina Beek. Among us, we have over 99 years of experience covering cybersecurity. That's pretty striking considering the industry hasn't even been around that long.
